analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for federal officers and prison staff to negligently deny urgent medical care to someone in custody.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime — punishable by up to a year in prison — for federal law enforcement officers, prison staff, and U.S. Marshals to negligently fail to get medical help for someone in their custody who is showing medical distress and suffers harm as a result. It would require an Inspector General investigation of every such incident, a confidential complaint system, and training for officers. It applied only to federal custody, not to state or local police.
analysis.who_benefits: People in federal custody — federal prisoners, detainees held by the Marshals Service, and anyone arrested by federal agents — would gain a legally enforceable right to immediate medical attention when they show medical distress, plus a confidential way to complain to an Inspector General and mandatory training for the officers guarding them. Their families would gain a path to investigation and prosecution when neglect causes unnecessary pain, injury, or death.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful — with a fine, up to one year in prison, or both — for a federal officer, Bureau of Prisons employee, or U.S. Marshal to negligently fail to get immediate medical attention for a person in custody displaying medical distress, including breathing difficulties, when that failure causes unnecessary pain, injury, or death.

Requires the relevant Inspector General to investigate every incident where a covered official's failure to get medical help causes unnecessary pain, injury, or death, and to refer negligent cases to the Attorney General for prosecution.
Creates a confidential complaint process so people in custody, staff, or others can report denial-of-care incidents to an Inspector General without going through the agency being accused.
Requires agency heads to train all covered officers on obtaining or providing medical assistance to people in medical distress, aiming to prevent deaths before they happen.
Lets a state attorney general sue in federal court for equitable and declaratory relief when a state resident is aggrieved by a violation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement officers, Bureau of Prisons staff, and U.S. Marshals would bear the cost: a new federal crime (a fine, up to a year in prison, or both) for negligently failing to get medical help, mandatory Inspector General investigations into failures that cause harm, required medical-distress training, and possible civil suits brought by state attorneys general. The agencies themselves would absorb the cost of training and complaint systems.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal law enforcement and prison officials

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only federal custody — federal agents, Bureau of Prisons, and Marshals — even though the death it is named for involved city police, leaving most policing deaths of this kind untouched.
The maximum penalty is one year in prison and a fine, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is a light sentence for a failure that results in death.

The law requires proving negligence and that the failure caused unnecessary pain, injury, or death — a high evidentiary bar in deaths that occur behind closed doors, and the bill adds no independent medical staffing or monitoring requirements that would prevent distress in the first place.
The state civil-enforcement provision allows only equitable and declaratory relief, not damages, so aggrieved families get no monetary remedy from it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: people die in custody after begging for help, and the bill would attach a personal legal consequence to ignoring medical distress, plus create an investigation and complaint trail after every such death. The costs fall on a specific group — federal officers and agencies — in the form of liability, investigations, and training. The main design weakness is reach and teeth: it covers only federal custody while most such deaths involve state and local police, and a one-year maximum penalty with a negligence standard is a modest deterrent. Still, on the core question of whose interests it serves, it clearly sides with the people in custody over the officers holding them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last month of the Congress and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2024, in the final month of a Congress whose term ended January 3, 2025, leaving almost no runway for action.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, from either party.

The bill's namesake, Andrew Kearse, died in 2017 after telling police he could not breathe; the legislation as written covered federal officers and prison staff, not the local police involved in his death.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement and prison officials are better off: no new criminal liability, no mandatory investigations, and no new training or complaint requirements were created. People in federal custody gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal officers face no new accountability

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a second sponsor, so no party split appears in the record; it was introduced by a Democrat and died in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and corrections officers and agencies
industries.note: The bill creates personal criminal liability for negligently denying medical care, requires agency Inspectors General to investigate failures that cause harm, and mandates medical-distress training. In this bill the industry's interest in avoiding liability runs against the safety of the people it holds.
